content: To enable the collection of nationally representative estimates of pretreatment HIV drug resistance (HIVDR), including resistance to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) among adults initiating first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART), countries are encouraged to implement or plan pretreatment HIVDR surveys. Between 2014 and 2017, 19 countries conducted such surveys, with an additional 17 surveys planned in 22 countries by 2017. These surveys are critical for informing public health responses to pretreatment HIVDR, as outlined in the WHO guidelines. A country’s response to pretreatment HIVDR should be based on robust national data. To determine the urgency of a public health response to NNRTI pretreatment HIVDR, countries should assess all available data, strive to obtain nationally representative data, and use these data to guide decisions about first-line ART regimens. Countries lacking national prevalence data on pretreatment HIVDR should urgently collect this information. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of people-centered care within HIV programs, guided by the promotion and protection of human rights and gender equality. This approach ensures that care is tailored to the needs of individuals while addressing broader social determinants of health. For individuals at higher risk of pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs, such as those with prior exposure to NNRTIs, initiating a non-NNRTI-containing regimen in first-line ART is recommended without requiring pretreatment HIVDR testing. Monitoring factors associated with the emergence of HIVDR at treatment sites, such as early-warning indicators, is essential. Annual monitoring of these indicators helps assess ART program performance, including adherence, retention, viral load suppression, and timely switches to second-line ART when indicated. Expanding viral load monitoring capacity is crucial to ensure that testing is accessible to all and that providers promptly switch patients to second-line ART upon confirmed viral failure (viral load > 1000 copies/mL). Strengthening treatment literacy, adherence support, and retention in care is also vital to minimize loss to follow-up and optimize program outcomes. Introducing new medicines or diagnostic products in HIV programs is a complex process requiring careful planning and coordination among policymakers, procurement managers, and manufacturers. WHO provides additional guidance on transitioning to dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimens and strategies for improving the quality of HIV care services at all levels. Nationally representative pretreatment HIVDR surveys are a high-priority activity for countries scaling up ART and should be repeated every three years. These surveys estimate the prevalence of HIVDR among ART initiators, regardless of prior antiretroviral (ARV) drug exposure, and among those without prior exposure. The surveys also assess the proportion of individuals starting or restarting first-line ART with prior ARV drug exposure and the prevalence of HIVDR in this group. Operationally, pretreatment HIVDR surveys enroll eligible individuals initiating ART during a predetermined period, collecting data on prior ARV drug exposure and stratifying the sample to calculate outcomes of interest. Prior ARV drug exposure is classified as “yes,” “no,” or “unknown” and further categorized by type of exposure, such as prior ART, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), or prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT). For infants under 18 months newly diagnosed with HIV, pretreatment HIVDR surveys assess the prevalence of resistance using dried blood spots collected during early infant diagnosis. These surveys inform the selection of standard firstand second-line ART regimens for children. Key research gaps identified by the WHO Guideline Development Group include the need for HIVDR surveillance for integrase inhibitors as programs transition to DTG-based regimens, data on HIVDR in key populations (e.g., children, pregnant women, men who have sex with men, female sex workers, and people who inject drugs), and methods to identify HIVDR transmission hotspots. Studies are also needed to evaluate the long-term efficacy and safety of DTG, the impact of pretreatment HIVDR on DTG-based regimens, and the clinical implications of specific resistance mutations. Implementation science research should focus on best practices for phasing in DTG in lowand middle-income countries to optimize population outcomes and minimize drug resistance. Prevention of HIVDR remains a cornerstone of global ART program success, requiring innovative strategies and targeted interventions.
